title: The moral argument
note: Moral arguments claim God best explains the moral order: objective values, binding duties, moral knowledge, or the rational hope that goodness and happiness meet. Kant argued practically, Newman from conscience, Craig deductively. The main objections are the Euthyphro dilemma and godless moral realism; the main replies ground goodness in God's nature and obligation in his commands.

read.title: Values, duties, and the Euthyphro
text: William Lane Craig's moral argument is a simple modus tollens:
(1) If God does not exist, objective moral values and duties do not exist. (2) Objective moral values and duties do exist. (3) Therefore, God exists.

'Objective' here means binding whether or not anyone believes it. The torture of a child for fun would be wrong even if everyone approved. Craig supports premise (1) by arguing that, on naturalism, humans are accidental products of evolution, with no standard of value beyond themselves and no lawgiver to issue duties.

The oldest objection comes from Plato's Euthyphro. Is something good because God commands it, or does God command it because it is good? If the first, morality looks arbitrary: God could have commanded cruelty. If the second, goodness seems to be a standard independent of God, which he merely reports.

Theists such as Robert Adams and William Alston reply that the dilemma is false. Goodness is grounded not in God's commands but in God's own essentially good nature, which is the standard of goodness. Duties, in turn, are constituted by the commands of this good God. His commands are therefore neither arbitrary nor answerable to a standard outside him.
Critics such as Erik Wielenberg reply that the theist simply stops the regress at God, and the atheist may just as well stop it at basic, necessary moral facts.

q.q: What form does Craig's argument take?
On the theistic reply, what is goodness grounded in?

o: An atheist can stop the regress at necessary moral facts
The Euthyphro dilemma has no answer
